records.bodyText:
Mill Rig Windfarm located near Darvel on the border of South Lanarkshire and East Ayrshire in Scotland, developed by OnPath Energy.
Key Specifications:
• Capacity: 33.4 MW to 36 MW
• Turbines: 6 Nordex N163/5.X turbines with a tip height of up to 199.5m to 250m.
• Record-Breaking Blades: Features 80-metre-long blades, marking some of the longest blades ever installed at a UK onshore wind farm.
• Power Output: Generates enough clean electricity to power more than 45,000 homes annually.
• Carbon Reduction: Displaces approximately 27,000 tonnes of CO2 each year.
• Lifespan: Designed for a 30-year operational period.
Construction was by main contractor RJ McLeod, with civil engineering and supply chain support from local partners like Hillhouse Quarry Group and technical project oversight by Natural Power.
Set for full commissioning and energisation in 2026.
The Mill Rig Community Fund will be launching later this year when Mill Rig is fully commissioned. Funds will total approx. £167,000 per year, rising every year with inflation, and local organisations and community groups can apply for up to £20,000 to support their projects.— in Darvel.

records.bodyText:
Documents uncovered through freedom of information by a campaign group have revealed that the Scottish Government was warned by a senior civil servant of risks, including ‘rising energy bills for locals’, from green AI data centres.
An email to one of the government’s working groups describes the need for a ‘clear system to protect locals’ and also warns of possible water shortages.
Campaigners have reacted with infuriation, noting that the civil servant " was highlighting very significant concerns back in March, and yet nothing seems to have filtered through".
The FOI of communications from the Green Data Centre and AI Growth Zone Crosscutting Working Group, covering the period from November 2025 to June 2026, included this email amongst other documents.
READ MORE:
Can communities benefit from hyperscale data centre boom?
What will be in new data centre guidance? Minister reveals
Sam Heughan reveals why he is 'against AI' and data centres
The email, from a senior civil servant, the Deputy Director of Domestic Climate Change at the Scottish Government’s Directorate for Energy and Climate Change, highlights a number of risks.
The letter states that "there are clearly significant impacts and risks and, considering our experience of just transition work over the last few years, I have various concerns about the way forward".
(Image: Jane Barlow/PA Wire)
It talks about the likelihood of "rising energy bills for locals", saying: "There is a clear just transition risk here, considering the prevalence of fuel poverty in the country already- and I’m conscious that is about to get worse as energy bills rise in the wake of the middle east conflict."
It also notes that, depending on location, there is a risk “that locals bear the brunt of increased electricity prices- or even a shortage of energy, or unreliable power- while seeing little direct benefit from ‘hosting’ the data centre."
The deputy director, name redacted, therefore suggests that there needs to be “a really clear system for protecting locals from increased energy prices and power shortages, as part of a deal to host the centre”. “That’s not just about grid upgrades,” the email says, “it’s about demand and supply."
Since this email was sent in March, local opposition to Scottish AI data centres has gathered into a national campaign, prompting tougher environmental scrutiny and a government planning pause while new national guidance is developed.
The email also observes that water is an issue: "The hard fact is that, even taking data centres completely out of the equation, Scotland is facing water shortages in multiple and growing parts of the country, due to climate change."
"Last year, water shortages in some parts of the country started in April- the earliest ever. And some rivers are already under strain from multiple industries (renewable energy, whisky, agriculture) so that fisheries, biodiversity and the environment are destroyed downstream."
The email notes: “Those effects are already set to become much worse. Add a water-hungry data centre and, even if it is comparatively efficient, it could badly impact other water dependent industries and livelihoods.”
The deputy director adds that “in Australia, data centre construction is dependent on guarantees of proportional work like reservoir investment and other management” and that this “seems like a really fruitful route to explore."
“I would also suggest that planning and impacts assessments take account of the latest Met Office assessments of weather changes to come,” the email adds, “we shouldn’t erroneously start from a baseline of current water availability, but we should build in future increasing shortages.
Anti-data centre campaigners have reacted to the contents of the FOI with “infuriation”.
Lisa Beacham, founder of the Hurlford campaign, said: “The revelation that our energy prices will be most likely increased to host these things while risking our general health is nothing short of exploitation of a deprived area.
"We have been raising the alarm about the potential impacts of hyperscale AI data centres in our communities for months and months while being completely ignored by the Scottish Government. To find out that a senior civil servant has raised issues that also concern us like energy prices, water use and climate emissions shows that the Government are aware of these issues, they are just covering them up.
She added: "Fuel poverty is a real concern for people in our own community and all over Scotland. If the Scottish Government knows about this issue of increasing energy prices and still are ploughing onward with giant data centres, it is an outrage and a grave injustice for everyone struggling to pay energy prices which are already amongst the most expensive in Europe."
Beacham also expressed concern over water shortages. “We have been told by Mark Wilson from ILI Group that water is a non-problem for Scotland while this FOI tells otherwise. Scotland's water resources are dwindling. If the Government wanted to placate us, this has just given us even more motivation.”
(Image: Colin Mearns)
Kat Jones, director of the charity Action to Protect Rural Scotland, said: "It is clear that the Scottish Government simply hasn't considered the climate in their rush to roll out the red carpet for hyperscale AI data centres."
"The Deputy Director was highlighting very significant concerns back in March, and yet nothing seems to have filtered through to local authorities, nor to the MSPs who have been advocating about exactly this on behalf of their local communities.
"This is an area where we have been actively working now for nearly a year and we have never seen any communications from the government nor seen any report or letter where these impacts are even acknowledged. It seems like the Scottish Government have been stonewalling the Deputy Director for Domestic Climate as effectively as they have been stonewalling communities and environmental campaigners."
A Scottish Government spokesperson said: “The Scottish Government will be publishing new planning guidance on data centres before the end of the year.
“Planning authorities are also now required to notify ministers of new data centre applications, with a new planning direction also requiring an Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) to be submitted during planning for all new data centres with a power capacity exceeding 50 megawatts (MW).
“Data centres represent a rapidly emerging sector and planning has an important role to play in considering applications, harnessing economic opportunities, and finding solutions which align with our climate goals.”

records.bodyText:
Kincardine & Longannet Ash Lagoons
Longannet Power Station was built on ash lagoons located in the Forth Estuary created by the Pulverised Fuel Ash (PFA) mixed with water and pumped too and allowed to settle to create new land in 1950/60s.
A similar process was followed with creation of the Valleyfield Ash Lagoons, which included Preston Island within the reclaimed land.
Preston Island in Torry Bay, Fife, was built on half-tide rocks around 1800 by Sir Robert Preston, to mine coal and fire salt pans boiling sea water. The mine closed after a deadly firedamp explosion in 1811, and salt-making seems to have ended by about the 1850s. On this 1969 map it still sits out in the tidal Forth. From 1970, ash slurry from Longannet power station was pumped into lagoons around it, and today a path from Low Valleyfield leads to the ruins.
The concrete ash slurry pipe holders snake their way across the landscape between the former Kincardine and Longannet Power Stations heading to Preston Island. Surviving pipes are rare now but tucked up against a fence usually obscured in long grass lies a section complete with slurry.
Pulverised Fuel Ash (PFA) collected from flue gas in the precipitators hoppers was mixed with river water and pumped to the ash lagoons at Longannet & Valleyfield to reclaim land from shore of the Forth Estuary.
Longannet and Cockenzie Ash Lagoons
Remediating the two former power station ash lagoons and creating important wetland habitats.
Since the closure of the coal-fired Power Stations at Cockenzie in 2013, and Longannet three years later, the ash lagoons, where residual ash slurry from the power generation process was deposited under water. The lagoons present a continual maintenance issue for Scottish Power, with prolonged dry weather raising concerns about windblown ash for local residents.
The first requirement was the draining of the lagoons, followed by reprofiling, removal of dust suppression, ash slurry pipes, and other infrastructure. Import material that would cap off the lagoons. Once capping was complete, a nature reserve wetland was created at Longannet with new footpath networks, benches and bird hides.
The works were carried out by I&H Brown with a total value of £8.5M with a project duration of 104 weeks.
Planning constraints at Low Valleyfield significantly reduced the volume of material that can be imported daily into the site through limiting vehicle movement to a prescribed level. We therefore monitored progress daily to ensure that sufficient imported material was always available to cap ‘open’ areas and minimise the probability of windblown ash becoming a concern.
A volume of 86,000m3 of material needed to be imported to complete the capping of the lagoon. A local source of suitable material that met the specification, which ironically was a coal mining by-product in the form of coillery shale.
The use of this locally sourced material significantly reduced road haulage distances and carbon emissions generated by the works, as well as being the most sustainable way to achieve the desired outcome.
As an alternative to a landfill disposal of the 9km long ash slurry pipe network at Longannet. The original concrete ash slurry pipework had been replaced during the life of the power station with HDPE pipework. This material was recycled off-site which facilitated the manufacture of new HDPE products for the industry.
— at Ash Lagoons, Low Valleyfield.

Inch Cape Offshore Windfarm will be £3.5 billion investment in the energy infrastructure and will create thousands of jobs during construction. Once operational it will generate more than 5TWh of renewable electricity each year and make a substantial contribution to the energy security.
Inch Cape Offshore Wind Limited is a 50/50 equal joint venture between ESB and Red Rock Renewables.
The onshore substation is located on the site of the old Cockenzie Power Station and connects to same grid substation that Cockenzie was connected to 1960s.— in Cockenzie, East Lothian, United Kingdom.

F/V Mistress: "Optics" and Political Damage Control
F/V Mistress ; Search & Investgation
The U.S. Coast Guard closed the active search and case for the commercial fishing vessel F/V Mistress "within three days" of its sinking on January 1, 2019. Helicopter response: A Coast Guard helicopter responding to the Mayday call aborted its search and returned after roughly 37 minutes due to high winds, poor visibility, low cloud ceilings, and radar/navigational hazards around the Block Island Wind Farm.
Federal agencies are aware the F/V Mistress is next to Block Island turbine # 1 . Reopening the case poses a political liability because it challenges the safety narratives surrounding offshore wind infrastructure

Latitude Air Ambulance Gulfstream G100 : Search & Investigation
The U.S. Coast Guard closed the active search and case for the private jet Latitude Air Ambulance Gulfstream G100 "within thirty days" of its sinking on October 3, 2026. The Transportation Safety Board (TSB) of Canada announced on November 2, 2026, that it had successfully located and recovered the aircraft's cockpit voice recorder (black box) and the upper third of the cockpit from the sea floor.
The exhaustive, multi-week search and recovery operation of the Air Ambulance serves as a high-visibility effort to counter accusations that the government is ignoring maritime and aviation safety hazards surrounding turbine layouts. Green Oceans notified federal agencies more than 60 days ago about the F/V Mistress's location next to the turbine. The response: "Crickets"
